metadata.title: Why Is Wall Street Doubting Google Stock?

content.text:
After a sharp pullback, one of the world's most dominant companies is trading at a steep discount to the market, forcing investors to decide if they are looking at a bargain or a warning sign.
Alphabet (GOOGL), the digital titan behind Google Search and YouTube, trades at 17.0 times earnings while the S&P 500 median sits at 23.5. That discount follows a real markdown; the stock is 15% below its 52-week high. Yet even with that pullback, shares have returned +65% over the past year, handily beating the S&P 500's +20% gain. The numbers present a paradox for bargain hunters. Is this a rare chance to own a quality business for less, or is the market correctly pricing in a coming storm?
The Business Is Firing On All Cylinders.
The case for value begins with operational strength. A quantitative screen for signs of a deteriorating business comes up empty. Alphabet's revenue over the last twelve months grew 20%, more than double the S&P 500 median of 8.4%, and comfortably outpacing its own three-year average of 15.5%. Profitability is elite, not merely intact. The company's operating margin over the last twelve months was 33%, far outpacing the S&P 500 median of 18.5%.
This performance is reflected across the business. The latest quarterly results show the growth engine is broad-based. The core Search and other segment grew 17%, YouTube ads climbed 13%, and the Google Cloud division posted a stunning 82% revenue increase. This performance is powered by what management calls "strong demand for AI infrastructure and AI solutions," a sign that its large investments are finding a receptive market.
The Market Is Pricing In The Cost Of An AI Arms Race.
If the business is so healthy, why the discount? The market's anxiety centers on the large cost of competing in artificial intelligence. Alphabet's stepped-up capital investments resulted in a negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion. Management has also raised its full-year 2026 capital expenditure guidance to a range of $195 billion to $205 billion, warning that free cash flow will "remain under pressure."
This spending spree fuels the central worry for skeptics: that Alphabet is paying a fortune to potentially fall behind. On its latest earnings call, analysts pressed management on the "speed of model releases" and whether its Gemini models can "remain at the frontier" against fast-moving competitors. The concern among some market observers is whether frontier AI investments will generate sufficient returns to justify the elevated capital intensity.
